justifications.functional_suitability: Fraud Scoring Engine handles R-01 decisions, and Case Management Backend with React UI covers R-02 case management. However, R-03 (updating rules and models without downtime) lacks an explicit hot-reloading or shadow-deployment mechanism, referencing only Database Migration Manager for schema updates.
justifications.performance_efficiency: The Go-based Fraud Scoring Engine uses Feature Cache (AWS ElastiCache for Redis) for sub-millisecond lookups and offloads audit writes asynchronously via Message Queue (Amazon SQS), keeping the critical path well within 50 ms P99 at 3,000 TPS.
justifications.compatibility: Standard protocols are defined cleanly: gRPC/mTLS with Payment Gateway, OIDC/OAuth2 via AWS Cognito for Identity Providers, Redis RESP, and standard AWS SDK integrations for SQS, KMS, and S3 Object Lock.
justifications.usability: React UI connected to Case Query Controller provides fraud analysts with dedicated interfaces for reviewing flagged cases, authenticated via AWS Cognito. Operational dashboards are also provided for monitoring.
justifications.reliability: API Router & Fallback Handler provides fail-open capabilities to avoid blocking payments beyond 1 minute. Amazon SQS and fraud-decisions-dlq protect against data loss in audit log ingestion, though multi-AZ deployment details remain implicit.
justifications.security: Addresses PCI-DSS and audit constraints through AWS WAF, tokenization at AWS API Gateway/NLB, mTLS/TLS 1.3, SQS KMS encryption, and Storage Writer Component writing to Tamper-Evident Storage (S3 Object Lock Compliance Mode).
justifications.maintainability: Well-decoupled microservices (Fraud Scoring Engine, Case Management Backend, Feature Store) using managed services align well with a small three-engineer team. However, model deployment lifecycle components are not explicitly separated from scoring logic.
justifications.portability: While targeted specifically for AWS eu-west-1, the architecture heavily couples key behaviors to proprietary AWS services (S3 Object Lock, SQS, KMS, ElastiCache, Cognito), limiting adaptability or migration to other environments.

PERF-01.justification: The Go scoring engine uses in-memory evaluation and low-latency Redis feature caching, decoupling audit emission via asynchronous SQS to achieve sub-50ms P99 latency at 3,000 rps.
elements: Scoring Evaluator with Feature Contribution Formatter
sensitivity_points: ElastiCache Redis read latency under high connection concurrency
Asynchronous SQS publish latency overhead on scoring worker threads
tradeoffs: Asynchronous audit logging sacrifices immediate read-after-write audit consistency for scoring throughput

PERF-02.justification: Case management workloads run on independent Spring Boot containers and Amazon RDS, completely isolating analyst query traffic from the Redis-backed Go scoring pipeline.
sensitivity_points: Physical separation of operational case databases and real-time feature caches
tradeoffs: Dual-store architecture increases operational complexity for a three-engineer team

AVAIL-01.justification: An API Router & Fallback Handler exists inside the scoring container, but an entire process crash or instance failure lacks an upstream edge-level automated fallback decision mechanism.
sensitivity_points: Edge gateway failover routing when backend scoring service fails health checks
tradeoffs: Approving payments on fallback reduces merchant decline rates but increases exposure to fraud

AVAIL-02.justification: Audit payloads are decoupled through buffered channels and Amazon SQS with DLQ support, preventing downstream S3/Lambda audit persistence slowdowns from impacting scoring latency.
sensitivity_points: SQS queue depth retention settings during prolonged storage outages
tradeoffs: Asynchronous buffering trade-offs instant audit persistence against bounded scoring latency

MOD-01.justification: The scoring evaluator formats feature contributions and records model versions, but no dynamic model hot-reloading, canary routing, or automated 5-minute rollback mechanism is specified.
elements: Scoring Evaluator with Feature Contribution Formatter
sensitivity_points: Model version tagging consistency across distributed Go scoring worker instances
tradeoffs: Static compilation in Go guarantees scoring performance but slows dynamic model deployment cycles

MOD-02.justification: The architecture records explainable rule contributions, but lacks an explicit runtime rule management engine or dynamic configuration ingestion mechanism to update rules without redeployment.
elements: Scoring Evaluator with Feature Contribution Formatter
sensitivity_points: Propagation delay of new velocity rules across feature store caches and scoring instances
tradeoffs: Embedding rule sets in compiled binaries increases execution speed but hinders sub-hour updates

SEC-01.justification: Ingress tokenization protects cardholder PANs from analyst view, and Cognito handles MFA/RBAC; however, automated behavioral anomaly detection alerting within 15 minutes is missing.
sensitivity_points: Tokenization enforcement boundary preventing clear-text PAN persistence in relational case tables
tradeoffs: Tokenization reduces PCI-DSS scope but requires token resolution overhead when resolving external disputes

SEC-02.justification: Amazon S3 Object Lock in Compliance Mode enforces 7-year WORM storage, KMS provides cryptographic signing, and the Relational Store's Audit Ledger Index enables fast retrieval.
sensitivity_points: Integrity of relational audit indices referencing immutable S3 object keys over 7 years
tradeoffs: Maintaining relational audit indices improves query response times while adding auxiliary storage maintenance
